paragraphs: What kind of act, in general terms, is the one that institutes government? To begin with, it is a complex act, made up of two others: establishing the law, and carrying it out.
In the first, the Sovereign decrees that a governing body will exist in this or that form. This act is clearly a law.

In the second, the people appoints the rulers who will be put in charge of the government just established. This appointment is a particular act, so it is clearly not a second law. It is only a consequence of the first, and a function of government.

The hard part is understanding how an act of government can happen before any government exists, and how the people, which is nothing but Sovereign or subjects, can in some circumstances become a prince or magistrates.

Here one of the astonishing properties of the body politic shows itself: it can reconcile operations that seem to contradict each other. It does this by suddenly turning sovereignty into democracy. Nothing visibly changes. Through nothing more than a new relation of all to all, the citizens become magistrates, moving from general acts to particular ones, from making law to carrying it out.

This change of relation is no theoretical hair-splitting without examples in practice. It happens every day in the English Parliament. On certain occasions the Lower House turns itself into a Grand Committee, to discuss business more effectively. One moment it is a sovereign court; the next it is a mere commission. It then reports to itself, as the House of Commons, what it did in Grand Committee, and debates all over again under one name what it has already settled under another.

Indeed, democratic government has this special advantage: it can be established in actual fact by a simple act of the general will. After that, the provisional government either stays in power, if that is the form adopted, or else sets up, in the Sovereign’s name, the government that the law prescribes. In this way everything proceeds regularly. There is no other legitimate way to set up a government that is consistent with the principles laid down so far.
